extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and researchers in media studies/communication and journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Frameworks and criteria for analyzing how ideology and power shape news content and news processes, including models (Marxist/political economy, propaganda model, Hallin's spheres), source structures, funding influences, and techniques by which media communicate deviance and maintain social control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological level analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how processes at lower levels (individual, routines, organization, extramedia) combine to produce ideologically related patterns of messages that serve higher power centers; ask in whose interests do routines and organizations ultimately work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This level takes an explicitly value-laden stance: researchers cannot avoid questions of power and interests. Studies at this level provide overarching context for analyses at lower levels and focus on how routines, values, and organizational structure maintain and reproduce a dominant ideology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical/Marxist research perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a Marxist/critical approach that emphasizes macro-cultural theorizing about power, class, and domination rather than positivist hypothesis-testing; sees media as implicated in class relations and ideological reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical scholars prefer qualitative, analytical, and philosophical methods. There is debate within the tradition over economic determinism vs greater media/message autonomy (political economy vs cultural studies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Media as social control and boundary maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how media function to integrate society by defining acceptable views/values (inside the bounds) and excluding or marginalizing others (read out of legitimacy), thereby maintaining social order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for routine presentation of 'normal' ideas in juxtaposition to portrayals of 'deviant' ideas; media's ability to 'define' situations confers ideological power and helps make existing orders appear natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: News selection dimensions of deviance
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate selection criteria in terms of deviance-related dimensions: controversial, sensational, prominent, and unusual events are more likely to be selected for coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings (Shoemaker et al.) show that events covered by U.S. media are often more deviant and/or more economically or politically significant to the United States; also that covered events may convey normative deviance relative to U.S. norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for communicating deviance and delegitimization
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify concrete techniques used to make actors/ideas appear deviant: trivialization; polarization (showing counterdemonstrations); emphasis on internal dissension; disparagement via undercounting/minimizing effectiveness; reliance on official sources; emphasis on presence of radicals/violence; selective visual framing and placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case examples (Gitlin; McLeod & Hertog) such as headlines that mischaracterize events, photos that emphasize confrontation, omission of participants' stated beliefs, and privileging officials' voices; these techniques serve ideological social control by minimizing perceived legitimacy of challengers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hallin's spheres model (consensus / legitimate controversy / deviance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify issues into three spheres: sphere of legitimate controversy (objectivity and balance sought; electoral contests, legislative debates), sphere of consensus (core values where journalists act as advocates/celebrants), and sphere of deviance (outsiders whom journalism exposes, condemns, or excludes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess journalists' roles and norms within each sphere and analyze who sets boundaries of acceptability; the model explains differential treatment and whether neutrality is maintained or abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political economy: ownership and profit-orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze how media ownership concentration, owner wealth, and profit orientation shape content and favor those with economic power; view media as part of the superstructure legitimating dominant interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use base/superstructure logic: ownership is a primary means of control; look for structural features (buyouts, conglomeration, erosion of business/news separation) that incline content toward capitalist interests and commodification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercialization / commodification of culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the tendency of media to treat cultural content as commodities, prioritizing lucrative markets and reallocating resources toward profitable nonnews information and sophisticated data gathering for corporate clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for shifts in resource allocation, emphasis on audiences/markets, and practices that improve profitability at the cost of broad information transmission (Schiller; Garnham).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variations in ideology by funding source (Altschull's four patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess ideological effects of different financing patterns: (1) official — state-controlled media reflect state ideology; (2) commercial — media reflect advertisers' and owners' ideology; (3) interest — content reflects financing group (political party/religious group); (4) informal — individual contributors promote personal views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the mix of these funding patterns across countries and time; the paymaster's ideology tends to shape content and access, with commercial paymasters dominating in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental / elite-theory influence and interconnections
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the interlocking relationships among media leaders and other elites (business, military, academia) and how circulation, shared schooling, board memberships, fellowships, and personnel exchange create class cohesion that facilitates media alignment with elite interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on Mills, Domhoff, Dreier: look for elite networks, fellowships, think-tank ties, and evidence that media critique is permitted only insofar as it preserves the broader system; such ties can produce a corporate-liberal philosophy and constrained adversarialism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite news source structure / source-network cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the structure of news sources (via network analysis): whether sources form a cohesive, centrally linked 'insiders' group across programs and issues (government officials, ex-officials, think-tank experts, journalists) versus pluralist prediction of multiple, issue-specific source sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize links by co-appearance on programs and map webs over time; strong cross-issue linkage supports the ideological/elite argument about privileged access and boundary-setting in political debate (Reese et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda model: five filters (Herman & Chomsky)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the five filters that bias news: (1) size/concentrated ownership/owner wealth/profit orientation; (2) advertising as primary income source; (3) reliance on information from government, business, and 'experts' funded/approved by power; (4) 'flak' as a disciplining mechanism; (5) 'anticommunism' (or equivalent ideological control mechanisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the filters to trace systemic pressures that make it difficult for alternative perspectives to gain access; empirical examples include covert 'white propaganda' operations and institutionalized source advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flak and organized monitoring as media discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider organized negative responses (complaints, threats, petitions, letters, monitoring groups) as instruments used to discipline and intimidate media into staying within acceptable elite viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify funding sources (foundations, think tanks) and monitors (e.g., Accuracy in Media) that produce flak; assess how flak shapes editorial caution and self-censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing debate within government-centric, two-party bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how media restrict public debate by organizing coverage primarily around governmental processes and a narrow political range (e.g., the two-party system), establishing a middle ground anchored by centrist or conservative experts and 'insider' journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for recurring formats that balance commentators within an acceptable comfort zone and incorporate dissent only insofar as it fits manageable, system-preserving discussion; this framing limits the scope of imaginable alternatives.
